item.dc:creator: S Dinakar
item.content:encoded: In the end, COP31 — a nearly two-week-long, UN-led global climate summit of around 200 nations — in Antalya, Turkey, proved a cop-out. Running into record extra time, nations failed to agree on a cover decision, a political but non-binding statement on the causes of and solutions to climate change and the provision of climate finance, for only the third time since the summit was first held in 1995.

US visa crackdown: Indian techies pack bags as American Dream fades Trump's immigration crackdown and tightening visa rules are prompting skilled Indian professionals to reconsider their future in the US, with some moving to the UK and other destinations

US visa crackdown

Surbhi Gloria Singh New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 2:54 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Skilled Indian professionals are increasingly reconsidering their future in the United States as changes to immigration and work visa rules under President Donald Trump make long-term career and residency plans harder to pursue, according to a Bloomberg report.   The administration has overhauled several immigration rules governing the entry and employment of foreign graduates and skilled workers, disrupting a system that had helped US companies attract engineers, researchers and other specialised talent from across the world.   Last week, the US Department of Labor proposed tighter rules for companies sponsoring foreign workers for permanent residency, adding to concerns among immigrants already facing uncertainty over their status and prospects of obtaining a green card.     Yash Sharma, 36, an Indian software engineer working at Google, has been on an H-1B visa for six years. He told Bloomberg that frequent policy changes and limited prospects of securing permanent residency or citizenship had made it increasingly difficult to concentrate on his work. The lengthy green card backlog for Indian nationals has further narrowed his options.   Describing the US as a "golden prison", Sharma said his application for an extraordinary ability visa was rejected after months of waiting. He has also avoided international travel for the past 18 months, fearing that he may not be allowed to re-enter the country. Also Read

He plans to move to the UK next month on a Global Talent visa, despite not having secured a job there. Even a return to the earlier immigration rules would not necessarily persuade him to stay, he told Bloomberg.   Another Indian professional, Swapnil Deshpande, a senior data analyst at a US technology company, moved to the country in 2018 to study at Northeastern University. He now questions whether the uncertainty and stress associated with staying in the US are worth the professional opportunities it offers.   Indian professionals reassess their US plans   The experiences reflect a wider concern among Indian professionals who have spent years building careers in the US but face uncertainty over their immigration status.   Earlier this year, Business Standard reported the case of Ajay Kumar Sharma, who had spent 16 years building a career in the information technology sector, working with companies such as Fidelity Investments and Bank of America.   He had lived and worked in the US for three years on an H-1B visa, with an established career and a clean immigration record. However, in April 2026, he and his wife and children had to return to India after his employer failed to complete the necessary paperwork on time, leaving him out of status.   In another case, Indian-origin data and artificial intelligence engineer Sunjana Ramana decided to leave the US after repeated unsuccessful attempts to secure an H-1B work visa.   In a LinkedIn post, Ramana said her decision was not driven by a lack of ambition or professional ability, but by an immigration system that left her with few options.   "Four-and-a-half years ago, I landed in the US with $80,000 in student debt and a stubborn belief in the American Dream," she wrote.   Instead of returning to India, Ramana plans to move to London and begin a new chapter in the UK.   US companies also rethink foreign hiring   The uncertainty is also affecting employers that have traditionally relied on international talent.   IBM told employees this month that it would stop sponsoring foreign workers for most positions in its consulting division, according to a document reviewed by Bloomberg. Affected employees have been told to relocate outside the US or leave the company by the end of the year.   Payments company Flywire is considering shifting some hiring to lower-cost markets. Microsoft, Adobe and several IT outsourcing companies have also been barred from a key green card sponsorship programme while officials investigate them, Bloomberg reported.   The Trump administration maintains that employers and foreign workers have abused the immigration system for years, turning a programme intended to bring in temporary specialised talent into a much larger hiring channel that has put downward pressure on wages for American workers.   A recent study by George J Borjas, a Harvard economist who served on Trump's Council of Economic Advisers found that skilled immigration reduces wages for college-educated US workers, supporting the administration's argument for tighter restrictions.   The policy changes are already reflected in immigration numbers. The US issued about 260,000 fewer temporary visas in the 2025 financial year than in the previous year, according to an analysis of federal data by the Migration Policy Institute. The Institute of International Education has also estimated that new international student enrolments fell by about 15% this autumn.   Reacting to the Bloomberg report on LinkedIn, recruiter Pradip Prashanna said skilled workers were unlikely to disappear simply because immigration routes had become more restrictive.   "Talent doesn't disappear, it relocates," he wrote, adding that companies capable of hiring and managing teams across borders through remote work, contract arrangements and offshore models would be better placed to attract top engineers.

item.content:encoded:

Can Nvidia preserve Jensen Huang's handshake deals after his departure? Elon Musk has warned that some of Nvidia's critical supply-chain deals could be at risk because they relied on personal agreements with Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang's exit raises concerns over Nvidia's informal deals with TSMC and other partners. (Photo: Reuters)

Barkha Mathur New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 23 2026 | 2:14 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Nvidia's business relationships with some of its biggest customers and suppliers are facing scrutiny following the departure of Jensen Huang . The concern is that some of these ties were built on personal relationships and verbal assurances rather than formal contracts, reported The Wall Street Journal .   According to the report, what was once seen as a strength of Huang's leadership could now become a vulnerability for the chipmaker. Investors are questioning whether Nvidia can maintain the business relationships and secure the supply-chain commitments that Huang built through his personal influence.   The issue came into focus after billionaire Elon Musk , whose companies SpaceX and Tesla are among Nvidia's major customers, flagged the risks associated with the company's relationship-driven approach.

"Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," Musk wrote in a post on X on November 14. He added that some critical agreements could be lost following Huang's departure.   According to The Wall Street Journal report, Huang had long regarded the absence of formal contracts with certain business partners as a reflection of the trust he had established across the supply chain. One prominent example is Nvidia's relationship with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which manufactures the chips designed by Nvidia.   Huang had spoken publicly about doing business with TSMC for nearly three decades without formal contracts. In a podcast interview in March, he said the two companies had conducted business worth tens and possibly hundreds of billions of dollars without a contract.

He reiterated the strength of the relationship in April, saying that while either company sometimes got a better deal than the other, their overall partnership remained strong.   However, the arrangement raises questions about how much of Nvidia's supply-chain security rests on relationships with its former chief rather than institutional agreements. The Wall Street Journal reported that while Huang may have relied on informal understandings with major partners, purchase orders and other agreements would have covered at least some of the underlying transactions.   Meanwhile, interim chief executive Colette Kress has sought to reassure investors that the company's relationships remain intact. During Nvidia's Q3 FY27 earnings call, Kress told analysts, "From a business perspective, it's business as usual." She added that the company remained engaged with its customers and suppliers.

She also highlighted Nvidia's purchase commitments worth $390 billion and referred to its relationship with TSMC, a critical manufacturing partner.   The company's reassurance comes amid calls from influential business and political figures for Huang's return. Musk has argued that his personal relationships are difficult to replace, while US President Donald Trump and other prominent figures have also supported his reinstatement. In a statement earlier this month, Huang indicated that he would be willing to return and said he had received calls from employees, investors, business partners and customers urging him to take back the top job. However, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones ruled out that possibility during the company's earnings call, saying the board had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him.

item.title: Oil, gas import bill up 60% in Oct as Brent surges, LPG use declines
item.description: Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: India's net oil and gas import bill rose 60 per cent year-on-year to $16 billion in October as Brent crude averaged $124.77 a barrel, almost double that of a year earlier, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), part of the oil ministry.The net bill was $10.0 billion in October 2025. Crude imports alone cost $19.5 billion, against $10.4 billion a year ago, even though volumes rose only 11 per cent to 23.3 million tonnes. LNG imports cost $1.3 billion, and petroleum product exports brought in $6.3 billion.Brent averaged $116.77 in September and $64.75 in October 2025. The Indian basket averaged $119.91 in October, against $65.08 a year earlier.Over April-October, the net import bill reached $97.7 billion, up from $70.3 billion a year earlier. Crude imports rose 2.7 per cent in volume but cost $111.0 billion, against $72.3 billion.Consumption of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) fell 12.3 per cent in October and 15.1 per cent in April-October. The number of active domestic LPG customers stood at 32.6 crore on November 1, down from 33.4 crore on April 1, the PPAC data showed.Direct private LPG imports fell 83.8 per cent in October and 97.3 per cent in April-October. Packed domestic LPG sales by state-run companies fell 11.8 per cent in October, and bulk LPG sales fell 49.1 per cent. Auto LPG sales rose 23.9 per cent.Imports of petroleum products fell 41.2 per cent in October and 49.3 per cent in the fiscal year so far. PPAC attributed the fiscal-year decline mainly to lower imports of LPG, pet coke and fuel oil.The International Energy Agency said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 that LPG imports fell by over 50 per cent in the first two months of shipping disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.Other fuels held up better. Diesel consumption rose 12 per cent in October to 8.5 million tonnes, petrol rose 3.5 per cent, and bitumen rose 16.5 per cent. Total petroleum product consumption rose 2.7 per cent to 20.5 million tonnes in October. It was still down 3.2 per cent in April-October at 134.2 million tonnes.Natural gas consumption fell 7.27 per cent to 5,707 million standard cubic metres in October. LNG imports fell 6.94 per cent to 3,014 million standard cubic metres.India processed 24.1 million tonnes of crude in October, up 7.1 per cent, or about 5.70 million barrels a day. Of that, 22.0 million tonnes were imported crude, and domestic output was 2.1 million tonnes. Imports met 88.7 per cent of crude consumption in October.Domestic crude and condensate output was 2.3 million tonnes. Import dependency for natural gas stood at 52.8 per cent in October.Ethanol blending in petrol stood at 20 per cent in October, PPAC data showed.
